newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major trawls for sceptical fishermen's votes.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major trawls for sceptical fishermen's votes.

text.p: A defiant John Major on Monday reaffirmed his determination to block an overhaul of the European Union's institutions unless Britain's partners agree to reform the bloc's fishing policies.
The British prime minister, facing deep divisions in his party over Europe, was taking a tougher stand on relations with the EU as he took his campaign for the May 1 election to southwest England.
The opposition Labour Party, which kicked off the week's electioneering by outlining its plans to improve the state education system, promised a more positive campaign.

Labour finance spokesman Gordon Brown said: "The Labour Party will not descend into the negative smear tactics that have identified the Conservative campaign...Our campaign will be positive, positive, positive."
Party officials deny Labour's new emphasis on a positive message signals that Conservative attacks last week have hit home, denting Labour's huge opinion poll lead.

Major made his latest campaign pledge after meeting fishermen angered by the EU's Common Fisheries Policy, which they say has encouraged foreign "quota-hopping" fishermen to grab an unfair share of declining British stocks.

As EU fisheries ministers met in Luxembourg to discuss plans for further deep cuts in quotas, Major said he was prepared to veto the bloc's long-running inter-governmental conference (IGC) when it concludes in Amsterdam in June.

"The IGC won't come to a successful conclusion until... the problem of quota-hopping is resolved satisfactorily," Major told a news conference in the neighbouring town of Penzance. "It cannot come to a solution without unanimity."
Major warned last year that he would block the IGC, crucial to EU's plans to expand from 15 members to more than 20 in the coming decade -- without a solution to quota-hopping.
This involves foreign trawlermen, predominantly Spanish, who have legally set up flag-of-convenience operations in England to buy licences that give them access to British fishing quotas.

But doubts about the government's resolve were raised when the Conservative Research Department, according to Monday's Guardian newspaper, reprimanded Defence Secretary Michael Portillo for saying the government was prepared to veto the IGC.
Major sides firmly with Portillo. "I happen to be prime minister, not the Conservative Research Department," he said.

Major said he was not issuing threats or being bloody-minded. But he said it was necessary to stand up for British interests, just as he did when he held out at the EU's Maastricht summit in 1991 for opt-outs from the social chapter on workplace rights and the proposed single currency.

Splits in the ruling Conservative party over Europe have dogged Major's 6-1/2 years as prime minister, but he was happy to take the offensive on the issue on Monday, accusing the opposition Labour and Liberal Democrat parties of being ready to sell out Britain to Brussels.

"In our country, if you are concerned about a too intrusive or centralised Europe, the only party you can safely vote for is the Conservative party. If you don't want a federal Europe, vote Conservative," he told reporters.

But down on the quay in Newlyn, one of Britain's busiest ports, fishermen were sceptical that Major -- or for that matter Labour leader Tony Blair, favourite to win the election -- could turn a tide they fear will capsize their industry.

There is strong support among the port's 3,000 fishermen for the Referendum party of Anglo-French businessman-politician Sir James Goldsmith, who last week launched his election campaign here. The harbour wall is garlanded with banners such as "Rule Britannia not Brussels" and "Save Our Fish 'n Ships".
Mick Mahon, a big, bearded fisherman in a Referendum party T-shirt, said all three main parties had let the industry down.

"Every time I see a British minister coming back from Brussels saying what a good deal I've got, I'm reminded of Neville Chamberlain coming back from Munich," he said, referring to the British prime minister who appeased Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler.
